title: The system: fleet telematics on a multi-DC Cassandra ring
caption: The ingest API writes each reading once at LOCAL_QUORUM; Cassandra copies it to the other region and to an analytics DC on its own, and a stream job watches the same readings for faults.

steps.text: Every truck sends a reading every 10 s: GPS position, speed, fuel level, coolant temperature, oil pressure. That is about 20 000 writes/s into a stateless ingest API, which validates them and drops exact duplicates.

The API inserts into readings_by_truck, partitioned by (vehicle_id, day) and clustered by timestamp, newest first. It also overwrites the truck's single row in latest_position, a different partition on its own replicas. The token-aware driver sends each write straight to one of its replicas; for this reading that is node B, which coordinates.
B appends to its commit log and memtable and forwards to A and C. With 2 of 3 local acks (LOCAL_QUORUM) it answers in a few milliseconds; there is no read before the write.
The same mutation goes to the other region's DC and to the analytics DC asynchronously. With RF 3 + 3 + 1, every row written lands on 7 replicas, and nobody waits for the far ones.

The API also publishes each reading to a stream. The alert job keeps a short window per truck and pages maintenance when, say, coolant stays too hot for five minutes. Cassandra is never polled for this.
Dispatchers watch the live map: it reads one latest_position row per truck in view. Monthly fuel and route reports run as Spark jobs on the analytics DC only, so full scans never touch serving nodes.

scenarios.name: Morning shift surge
scenarios.summary: At shift start most trucks power on together and upload what they buffered overnight. Writes are appends, so they stay fast; the bill comes later as compaction debt.

steps.text: Around 6 a.m. tens of thousands of trucks leave depots with poor signal and flush hours of buffered readings at once. The write rate jumps to several times normal.
Old readings go into their own day's partition with their original timestamps. Cassandra sorts by clustering key, so arriving late or out of order costs nothing extra.
Memtables flush more often and compaction falls behind; reads touch more SSTables and the map's p99 rises for a while.
The stream absorbs the burst for the alert job. Alerts on backfilled readings are marked as late so nobody is paged for a fault from last night.
Size the ring for the peak replicated write rate, and keep disk and CPU headroom so compaction can catch up.

scenarios.name: Link to DC2 down
scenarios.summary: LOCAL_QUORUM keeps DC1 writing during a cross-region outage; DC2 falls behind and is brought back with hints and repair.

steps.text: The cross-region link drops. DC1 nodes mark DC2 as unreachable.
Ingest keeps writing at LOCAL_QUORUM: two acks from DC1 are all it waits for, so trucks and the map notice nothing.
B stores hints for the writes DC2 missed, up to the hint window (3 hours by default).
Dispatchers served by DC2 see stale positions until it catches up. After a long outage, run repair so DC2 gets every reading the hints did not cover.

scenarios.name: Add node D to DC1
scenarios.summary: Adding capacity is an online operation: the new node streams its token ranges from the current replicas, then takes traffic.

steps.text: A new customer adds 40 000 trucks and DC1 disks are filling. An operator starts node D; it takes tokens on the ring and joins through gossip.
D streams the data for its new ranges from the replicas that own them today. Writes for those ranges also go to D while it joins.
Once streaming finishes, D serves reads and writes, and every node owns a smaller share.
Run cleanup on the old owners to delete the ranges they gave away; until then their disk usage doesn't drop.
